The fire-driven invasion model simulated by ForestFireR

Source: R/model.R
ForestFireR-model.Rd

Reference definition of the model this package simulates: two vegetation types, a native species and an invader, competing for space in a system where fire is the process that lets the invader win. The same transition rules are simulated in three ways – on an explicit lattice (simulate_spatial()), as the deterministic well-mixed limit (simulate_mean_field()), and as the well-mixed stochastic process at a finite population size (simulate_mean_field_stochastic()). This page defines the states, the transitions and every parameter the package's functions take.

States

Each site of an L x L lattice is in one of five states, coded as in FF_STATE:

codenamesymbolmeaning
1native\(V^{nat}\)native vegetation
2invader\(V^{inv}\)invading vegetation
3fire\(F\)burning
4empty\(\emptyset\)unoccupied, never burned
5empty_postfire\(\emptyset^F\)unoccupied, left behind by a fire

Both unoccupied states can be colonised by a vegetated neighbour, but only \(\emptyset^F\) additionally has the long-range post-fire regrowth channel (see eta_nat/eta_inv below). State \(\emptyset\) is produced only by vegetation death, whose rates the R interface fixes at zero, so it appears only if the initial landscape contains it.

The simulate functions report the densities n1..n5 (the fraction of sites in each state, in the order of the table) plus n0 = n4 + n5, the total unoccupied fraction. The five state densities sum to 1 at every recorded point.

Transitions

Sites change state in continuous time. On the lattice, \(v_X\) is the number of the site's four nearest neighbours (von Neumann neighbourhood, periodic boundaries by default) that are in state \(X\):

transitionrateset through
\(\emptyset \to V^{nat}\)\(\lambda_{\emptyset nat}\, v_{nat}\)L_01
\(\emptyset \to V^{inv}\)\(\lambda_{\emptyset inv}\, v_{inv}\)L_02
\(\emptyset^F \to V^{nat}\)\(\lambda_{\emptyset nat}\, v_{nat} + \lambda^{rg}_{nat}\)L_01, eta_nat
\(\emptyset^F \to V^{inv}\)\(\lambda_{\emptyset inv}\, v_{inv} + \lambda^{rg}_{inv}\)L_02, eta_inv
\(V^{nat} \to V^{inv}\)\(\lambda_{nat\,inv}\, v_{inv}\)L_12
\(V^{inv} \to V^{nat}\)\(\lambda_{inv\,nat}\, v_{nat}\)L_21
\(V^{nat} \to F\)\(\lambda^{ig}_{nat} + \lambda^{sp}_{nat}\, v_F\)Lig_13, xi_nat
\(V^{inv} \to F\)\(\lambda^{ig}_{inv} + \lambda^{sp}_{inv}\, v_F\)Lig_23, xi_inv
\(F \to \emptyset^F\)\(\lambda^{F\emptyset}\)L_30
\(V \to \emptyset\)\(\lambda_{nat\,\emptyset}\), \(\lambda_{inv\,\emptyset}\)fixed at 0

Colonisation, competitive replacement and fire spread are local: their rates are proportional to the matching neighbour count, so an isolated site is inert to them. Spontaneous ignition, fire burnout and long-range post-fire regrowth do not depend on the neighbourhood.

Dimensionless parametrisation

Fire spread and post-fire regrowth are supplied as probabilities rather than as rate constants, which keeps them comparable across parameter sets:

  • \(\xi_i = \lambda^{sp}_i / (\lambda^{sp}_i + \lambda^{F\emptyset})\) (xi_nat, xi_inv) is the probability that a burning neighbour sets a site of type \(i\) alight before that neighbour burns out. \(\xi = 0.5\) is the point where spread and burnout are equally fast.

  • \(\eta_i = \lambda^{rg}_i / (\lambda^{rg}_i + \lambda_{\emptyset nat})\) (eta_nat, eta_inv) is the probability that a post-fire site is taken by species \(i\)'s long-range regrowth rather than by ordinary colonisation. Both species use \(\lambda_{\emptyset nat}\) (L_01) as the reference rate.

xi2lambda() and eta2lambda() invert both relations, \(\lambda = \xi/(1-\xi)\,\lambda_{ref}\); every simulate function takes xi_*/eta_* and converts internally.

The initial landscape adds one more dimensionless parameter, the clustering p of the species placed on it (see generate_landscape()).

Baseline parameters and the invasion mechanism

default_rates() returns the baseline set, with time in years: \(\lambda_{\emptyset nat} = \lambda_{\emptyset inv} = 0.03\), \(\lambda_{nat\,inv} = 0.005\), \(\lambda_{inv\,nat} = 0.01\), \(\lambda^{F\emptyset} = 10^6\), \(\lambda^{ig}_{nat} = 0\), \(\lambda^{ig}_{inv} = 10^{-4}\), \(\xi_{nat} = 0.5\), \(\xi_{inv} = 0.6\), \(\eta_{nat} = 0\), \(\eta_{inv} = 0.6\).

These values make the competition asymmetric in the native species' favour: the native replaces the invader twice as fast as the reverse (\(\lambda_{inv\,nat} = 2 \lambda_{nat\,inv}\)), and the two colonise unoccupied space equally well, so without fire the invader cannot spread. All of its advantages act through fire: it is the only species that ignites spontaneously, it carries fire better (\(\xi_{inv} > \xi_{nat}\)), and it is the only one that regrows into post-fire sites through the long-range channel (\(\eta_{inv} > \eta_{nat} = 0\)). Fire converts native vegetation into \(\emptyset^F\), which the invader claims preferentially, which raises the amount of fire-prone vegetation: invasion and fire reinforce each other. \(\xi_{inv}\) and \(\eta_{inv}\) are the strength of that feedback, and are the parameters most analyses vary.

Fire is also much faster than vegetation: with \(\lambda^{F\emptyset} = 10^6\)/year a site burns for about half an hour, against the decades over which vegetation turns over. A single outbreak therefore resolves in a sliver of simulated time (see capture_fire_snapshots in simulate_spatial() for how to observe one).

Mean-field limit

simulate_mean_field() integrates the well-mixed limit of the same transitions, in which each neighbour count \(v_X\) is replaced by the global density \(n_X\):

$$\dot n_1 = \lambda_{\emptyset nat} n_1 (n_4 + n_5) + \lambda^{rg}_{nat} n_5 + \lambda_{inv\,nat} n_1 n_2 - \lambda_{nat\,inv} n_1 n_2 - (\lambda^{ig}_{nat} + \lambda^{sp}_{nat} n_3) n_1$$ $$\dot n_2 = \lambda_{\emptyset inv} n_2 (n_4 + n_5) + \lambda^{rg}_{inv} n_5 + \lambda_{nat\,inv} n_1 n_2 - \lambda_{inv\,nat} n_1 n_2 - (\lambda^{ig}_{inv} + \lambda^{sp}_{inv} n_3) n_2$$ $$\dot n_3 = (\lambda^{ig}_{nat} + \lambda^{sp}_{nat} n_3) n_1 + (\lambda^{ig}_{inv} + \lambda^{sp}_{inv} n_3) n_2 - \lambda^{F\emptyset} n_3$$ $$\dot n_4 = -(\lambda_{\emptyset nat} n_1 + \lambda_{\emptyset inv} n_2) n_4$$ $$\dot n_5 = \lambda^{F\emptyset} n_3 - (\lambda_{\emptyset nat} n_1 + \lambda_{\emptyset inv} n_2) n_5 - (\lambda^{rg}_{nat} + \lambda^{rg}_{inv}) n_5$$

(the vegetation death terms, zero in the R interface, are omitted). Fire enters as a continuous density: \(n_3\) settles at \((\lambda^{ig}_{nat} n_1 + \lambda^{ig}_{inv} n_2)/(\lambda^{F\emptyset} - \lambda^{sp}_{nat} n_1 - \lambda^{sp}_{inv} n_2)\), of order \(10^{-11}\) under the baseline parameters – tiny, but always burning, so the feedback runs continuously. In the lattice and finite-N versions fire is instead a discrete, rare event. That difference, rather than the presence or absence of space alone, is why the three engines can disagree.

The three engines

  • simulate_spatial() and simulate_spatial_from_grid(): the lattice continuous-time Markov chain, simulated exactly with the Gillespie algorithm. Boundaries are periodic unless periodic = FALSE.

  • simulate_mean_field(): the deterministic well-mixed limit above.

  • simulate_mean_field_stochastic(): the continuous-time Markov chain of the same well-mixed system with N individuals. Pairwise reactions have propensity \(\lambda N_i N_j / N\) and first-order reactions \(\lambda N_i\), so the process has the mean-field equations as its N -> infinity limit, with demographic stochasticity and discrete fire at finite N. Comparing it against simulate_spatial() at \(N = L^2\) separates the effect of spatial structure from that of demographic noise.

Initial landscapes

generate_landscape() places one species over a background of another with a prescribed density and clustering p; generate_landscape_layers() builds landscapes from a sequence of such placements over an arbitrary fill state. Both grow the pattern cell by cell while steering the neighbour pair statistics towards the targets set by p, in the spirit of the pair-correlation landscape generators of Hiebeler (2000).

Implementation notes

  • Gillespie event selection keeps the per-site total rates in a binary sum tree (engine = "tree", O(log N) per event). engine = "linear" is the cumulative scan over all sites, kept for reproducing runs made with ForestFireR < 0.7.0.

  • Random numbers come from the engine's own std::mt19937_64, independent of R's generator, and seeded per call from each function's seed argument (or from the clock when that is NULL). Set options(ForestFireR.rng = "legacy") to select the rand() generator of versions up to 0.7.x.

  • The mean-field system is stiff: the fire compartment is updated with its exact linear solution over each step while the vegetation block is integrated with classic RK4, which is stable for any practical step size at \(\lambda^{F\emptyset} = 10^6\).

  • A Gillespie step is applied in full, so the reported time_sim can exceed the requested T, by a wide margin when the total rate is low.

References

Saravia, L.A. and de la Fuente, R. Dynamics of invasion in forest-fire models (manuscript). Analysis code: https://github.com/EcoComplex/InvasionForestFiresBistability.

Gillespie, D.T. (1977) Exact stochastic simulation of coupled chemical reactions. Journal of Physical Chemistry 81, 2340-2361.

Hiebeler, D. (2000) Populations on fragmented landscapes with spatially structured heterogeneities: landscape generation and local dispersal. Ecology 81, 1629-1641.
